edges.description: Following entry, B. pseudomallei invades host cells and escapes into the cytosol.
Cytosolic bacteria recruit host actin for intracellular movement and spread.
Invasion and intracellular replication in lung tissue produce pneumonia, the most common focal presentation.
Cell-to-cell spread drives membrane fusion and multinucleated giant cell formation.
Intracellular replication and spread drive innate immune activation and systemic sepsis.
Persistent focal infection organises into abscesses in multiple organs.
Systemic infection and dysregulated innate immune activation manifest as sepsis.
Severe systemic infection progresses to septic shock.
Dissemination of B. pseudomallei into the bloodstream produces bacteraemia.
Innate immune activation and cytokine release produce fever.
Haematogenous seeding of the central nervous system produces neurological melioidosis.
Focal suppuration in the liver produces hepatic abscesses.
Focal suppuration in the spleen produces splenic abscesses.
Focal suppuration in the prostate produces prostatic abscesses.
Focal bone infection produces osteomyelitis.
Focal joint infection produces septic arthritis.
Cutaneous suppuration produces skin ulcers and subcutaneous abscesses.

Intrinsic resistance excludes most first-line antibiotics, leaving ceftazidime and the carbapenems as the viable PBP-directed options — the reason those specific agents, not penicillins, anchor the intensive phase.
Diabetes impairs neutrophil/innate immune defence, so an inoculum a healthy host would clear instead establishes invasive, frequently septic infection.
Renal disease is an established host predisposing factor for invasive melioidosis.
Thalassemia is an established host predisposing factor for melioidosis.
Alcoholism is an established host predisposing factor for invasive melioidosis.
Chronic lung disease is an established host predisposing factor for melioidosis.
Contact with contaminated soil and water is the route by which B. pseudomallei enters the host.

nodes.description: Unlike classic obligate intracellular pathogens, B. pseudomallei is fully susceptible to the cell-wall-active beta-lactams (ceftazidime, carbapenems) that anchor the acute intensive phase. Its facultative intracellular persistence instead gates the second, eradication phase: because surviving intracellular organisms drive relapse and recrudescence, cure requires months of oral therapy with cell-penetrant agents (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with doxycycline as an alternative) that reach the intracellular niche.

nodes.description: B. pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotic classes (aminoglycosides, penicillins, polymyxins, macrolides), in large part through multidrug efflux pumps of the resistance-nodulation-cell-division (RND) family such as AmrAB-OprA. This intrinsic resistance narrows effective therapy to ceftazidime, the carbapenems, and co-trimoxazole.
